slides.title: What is Storm Water Pollution?
slides.description:
Results from materials and chemicals washed into storm drains from streets, gutters, industrial sites, parking lots, etc.

It is significant because storm water is untreated and flows directly into lakes and the ocean

Affects water quality, resulting in closed beaches Hurts aquatic life

Improper disposal of chemicals will result in fines to the dealership

slides.title: Why do We Need to be Aware of Storm Water Pollution?
slides.description:
EPA estimates that:

  • Used oil from a single oil change can pollute up to 1 million gallons of fresh water
  • American households alone generate 193 million gallons of used oil every year
  • The equivalent of 17 Exxon Valdez oil spills is improperly dumped every year

slides.title: Waste Generated at Dealerships
slides.description:
Solvents (paint and thinners)

antifreeze

Brake fluid and brake lining

batteries

motor oils

Fuels (gasoline, kerosene, diesel)

Lubricating grease

slides.title: Waste Water Generated
slides.description:
Waste water from floor washing

Spent coolant discharges

Spilled materials

Vehicle-washing and engine cleaning tanks

Waste water from water-based, parts-cleaning tanks

Most waste water from service bays enter drains, go into a grit chamber, then an oil/water separator before entering the public water treatment pipes

slides.title: Wastewater Pollution-Prevention Methods
slides.description:
Do not drain or replace oil, coolant or other vehicle fluids on the ground or outside pavement

Do not steam clean engines outdoors

Prevent chemical spills in service bays; when they occur, clean up immediately and thoroughly

Dry-sweep floors before wet cleaning and don’t sweep floorwashings from service to outside pavement

If you see a release of fuel, oil or other hazmat, report it to a supervisor

Know how to use absorbents and spill-cleanup materials for immediate response to any indoor or outdoor spills

Make sure the used-oil transporter cleans up any spills during pump-out of used oil tanks

slides.title: Vehicle Washing Requirements
slides.description:
Wash areas should be located on impervious surfaces with drains piped to disposal devices

It is recommended that washing areas be enclosed, but at a minimum, floors should be graded to allow wash water to drain

Absorbents should be used if an oily sheen appears

A recycle system that recycles both wash water and rinse water, with no discharge of wastewater to waters of the State, should be considered.

slides.title: Used Oil Storage
slides.description:
Above ground tanks with capacity of 660 gallons or more are subject to federal regulations

Collection drums must be covered and labeled, in good condition and secured from vandals, and in compliance with local fire codes.

Label drums, tanks and fill pipes with the words “Used Oil”. “No Smoking” signs should be posted in used oil storage areas

A concrete or impervious floor with diking is required to prevent stormwater and rainfall contact

Immediately clean up spills of used oil with absorbents and properly dispose of the spent materials

slides.title: Transportation of Used Oil
slides.description:
Used oil shipped off site must be picked up by transporters with EPA ID numbers

This applies to filters and oily rags

Keep logs or records of off-site shipments of used oil

slides.title: Mixing Other Materials with Used Oil
slides.description:
Only other materials defined as used oil may be mixed with used oil, examples:

  • Transmission and hydraulic fluids
  • Petroleum-based, non-hazardous lubricating fluids
  • Hydraulic, cutting, gear and cooling oils
  • Synthetic oils

Never mix gasoline, wastewater, a listed hazardous waste, an unknown waste, halogenated solvents or antifreeze with used oil

slides.title: Used Oil Filter Disposal/Recycling
slides.description:
Over 400 million used oil filters are generated in the US a year

To be disposed of, they must be properly treated. Recycling of used filters is becoming more common

Used oil filters are generally picked up by an EPA certified contractor and:

  • Shredded, cut open and solvent washed
  • Crushed into low-density pucks
  • Crushed into high-density briquettes
  • Burned directly in cement kilns
  • Recycled as scrap steel
  • Prepared for acceptable landfilling

slides.title: Absorbents Contaminated with Used Oil and other Materials
slides.description:
Materials used to absorb used-oil spills such as paper and cloth towels, and clay-based, cellulose-based, corncob, sawdust or other absorbents which contain “free-flowing oil” are considered used oil and must be treated as such.

“Free-flowing oil” means the material drips with used oil

If any materials with “free-flowing oil” are stored with other absorbents, all must be treated as used oil. Used absorbents should be stored in covered containers labeled “used oil wastes”

questions.question: In some cases is it OK to drain or replace oil, coolants or other vehicle fluids on the ground or outside pavements.
Dry sweep floors before wet cleaning and never sweep to the outside pavement.
If an oily sheen appears on your wet floors, what should you do?

answers.a: Mop up and dump down the nearest drain
answers.b: High pressure spray the area to insure oil dissipates properly
answers.c: Use absorbents materials to soak up the oil and dispose in proper containers
answers.d: Use rags and or any other cloth materials to soak up the water/oil area and throw away in any trash receptacle
